nitrogen_intensity_margin.status: WIRED AND WORKING at supply level; a SEPARATE market-loop defect now dominates
nitrogen_intensity_margin.note: Addresses the structural defect found by the Green Deal comparison: nutrient coefficients are FIXED per activity (SWHE 125.9 kg N/ha always), so a nitrogen constraint could only be met by cutting AREA, overstating the response ~10x against CAPRI (wheat -24% vs -1.9%). CAPRI'S MECHANISM (read from supply_model.gms): v_cropNutNeedMultFact is a free VARIABLE scaling each crop's nutrient need, so application per hectare flexes and the model trades fertiliser cost against yield; the adjustment splits between the intensity and extensive margins. IMPLEMENTED (capri_mod/supply/intensity.py): a per-crop intensity factor m in [m_min, 1] scaling N/ha, with a Mitscherlich yield response y(m) = y_base * (1-exp(-k*m))/(1-exp(-k)), normalised so y(1) = 1 EXACTLY - the base year is reproduced by construction, which is what protects PMP calibration when this is switched on. Under a binding ceiling, intensity is cut where revenue lost per kg N saved is LOWEST (not uniformly), so the adjustment falls on low-value crops first. VALIDATED: yield_factor(1.0) == 1.0 to 1e-12; response monotone with diminishing returns; a 20% N cut costs 4.3% yield (agronomically plausible, cf. N-response trials). On FR10 with a real regional ceiling: -0% not binding (intensity exactly 1.000, zero yield loss), -10% -> intensity 0.930 and 1.71% yield loss, -20% -> 0.868 and 3.24%. Previously a 5.6% N cut forced a -24% wheat AREA collapse; now a 20% cut costs 3.2% of yield with area largely intact. THE ONE ASSUMPTION: the curvature k (default 3.0) sets how fast yield falls as N is withdrawn. It is taken from the agronomic literature (k=3 gives ~5% yield loss for a 20% N cut on cereals), exposed as a parameter, and recorded as an assumption - it was NOT tuned to make the CAPRI comparison come out right. A BUG FOUND AND FIXED DURING BUILD: the descent loop's iteration budget was (1-m_min)/step, which lets only ONE crop reach the floor; the ceiling was silently left unmet and intensity barely moved (0.992 regardless of the cut). Budget now scales with the number of crops. NOT YET DONE: this is a standalone, tested response function. It is NOT yet called from SupplyModel.solve, so nitrogen scenarios still use the area-only path and the ~10x over-response stands until it is wired in. Wiring it means recomputing net revenues from the intensity-adjusted yields inside the solve, which touches the PMP objective and needs a base-fidelity re-check.
nitrogen_intensity_margin.wiring: WIRED into SupplyModel._solve_inner via _apply_intensity_margin(): when an N ceiling binds it picks the cost-minimising intensity, scales the N coefficients so the constraint sees the reduced application, and scales net revenues by the yield factor so the yield loss is paid for. nutrient_coefs added to the solve's backup/restore block - without it the reduced application leaked into every subsequent solve on the same model. BASE FIDELITY UNCHANGED: 11.35% in real-agriculture cells, identical to before wiring, and 248/248 regions still converge. At full intensity the yield factor is exactly 1.0, so an unbound ceiling is a true no-op - this is the property that makes the extension safe. SUPPLY-LEVEL RESULT (the fix works): a -10 kg N/ha ceiling on FR10 now moves SWHE by -0.1% instead of -24%. Wheat intensity falls to 0.960 (4% less N) for a 0.7% yield loss and the area barely moves - the adjustment sits on the INTENSITY margin, as in CAPRI. Verified two independent paths agree exactly: SupplyModule.run and direct SupplyModel.solve both give SWHE -0.72% across 25 regions. Constraint arithmetic confirmed: N use at base levels falls 104694 -> 98692 against a bound of 98817, so area no longer has to absorb the cut. REMAINING DEFECT, NOT THE INTENSITY MARGIN: at MODEL level the same scenario still gives SWHE -24.25%. Isolated to the MARKET loop - with max_outer_iter=1 it is already -21.61%, so it is the FIRST market pass, not iterative feedback. Supply changes by -0.72% and the market amplifies that into -24%. That is a market-module price-response defect, structurally separate from the nitrogen intensity question, and it will distort ANY scenario that perturbs supply - not just nitrogen ones. It is the next thing to diagnose; the ~60x Green Deal gap cannot be re-measured meaningfully until it is understood.

cap_double_counting_bug.note: Diagnosing why a 0.7% supply change became a 24% model-level response found a bug that had distorted EVERY scenario run through CAPRIModel. Prices barely moved (SWHE +1.0%) and a price rise should RAISE supply, so the amplification was not the market. With price_signals=None on iteration 1 the only difference was the policy dict: adders alone raised wheat +29.05% (1919.4 -> 2477.0) with NO nitrogen constraint; adding the N limit returned it to 1941.8, near the no-policy 1919.4. The '-21.6% nitrogen effect' was the constraint UNDOING an inflated baseline. ROOT CAUSE: calibrated net revenue already contains cap_premium (FR10 SWHE 490.1 of which 322.1 is CAP); get_supply_policy_adders() returns the ABSOLUTE payment (332.2) and _solve_inner ADDS it, nearly doubling CAP support. The same inflation sat in the BASELINE, so scenario-vs-baseline comparisons measured the double-count. FIX: model.py passes adders as a DELTA from the baseline policy, so BASELINE is a no-op and a scenario gets its own change (-100 EUR/ha BISS -> -125.0 on wheat). RESULT: nitrate -10 gives SWHE -0.77% at model level, matching the supply-level -0.72% exactly (was -24.25%); mean activity change 1.06% against CAPRI's ~1.2%. Regression test test_cap_support_not_double_counted added.

greendeal_reference_run_identification.status: the comparison target is probably NOT a full Green Deal run
greendeal_reference_run_identification.note: Re-examining the comparison from the beginning, starting from the SETA anomaly (CAPRI-mod +0.34% vs CAPRI -5.73% under a scenario that MANDATES 10% non-productive area). FINDING 1 - WE HAD THE INSTRUMENT WRONG (fixed). CAPRI's landscape.gms implements the Biodiversity Strategy 10% target as a FLOOR on the non-productive activity: data(ru,'FALL','FLOOR') = lndscpTarg/10 * setAsideTarget * UAAR + SETF. We had implemented it as a REDUCTION of available arable land. Those are different instruments: a floor forces land INTO fallow (SETA rises), whereas shrinking arable squeezes every crop proportionally and leaves SETA untouched. Reimplemented as a SETA floor sized on UAA; SETA now rises +202% for a 10% target (fallow is 2.72% of UAA at base, so roughly a tripling - arithmetically right). FINDING 2 - THE COMPARISON TARGET LOOKS WRONG. With the instrument corrected, CAPRI's own numbers still do not behave like a Green Deal run: (a) mineral fertiliser per UAA (UAAR/NITF) moves only 210.28 -> 208.06, i.e. -1.05%, against an F2F target of -20%; (b) FALL DECREASES 3.79% and SETA -5.73%, when a binding 10%-of-UAA landscape floor must push them UP (10% of UAAR 1111718 is ~111000 against a FALL of only 38943); (c) the whole increment averages 1.17% |change|, very small for a bundle this aggressive. MOST LIKELY EXPLANATION: greendeal_scenarios.gms line 192 encodes the active instruments in the scenario NAME (greendeal_lnds<X>_org<X>_pest<X>_mine<X>_surp<X>_diet<X>_oth<X>), and line 193 renames the all-instruments-off case to 'greendeal_reference'. The uploaded file was renamed to scen_greendeal_2030.txt on extraction, so those settings are lost. The evidence is consistent with the file being a greendeal REFERENCE (instruments off or near-off) rather than the policy scenario - in which case the ~1.17% we have been calibrating against is baseline drift between two reference variants, NOT a Green Deal policy effect. IMPLICATION: the magnitude comparison reported earlier (CAPRI-mod 2.7x CAPRI) may be comparing a real policy shock against a near-null run, which would make the apparent 2.7x meaningless in either direction. This must be resolved before any further calibration against this target. TO RESOLVE: the original CAPRI filename (which encodes lnds/org/pest/mine/surp/diet/oth settings) or the batch/GUI settings of that run. Without it we cannot know which instruments to replicate.

defect_list_items_6_and_8.note: ITEM #8 - HARD-CODED 2017 PATHS (fixed). capri_pmp.py had REGIONAL_FILE and PMP_ELAS_FILE as literal '2017/supply/...' paths. Re-basing the model to another year would have SILENTLY fallen back to the literature defaults - the CAPRI elasticities would simply stop being found, with no error and no warning. Both now go through the loaders' base-year-aware resolve_data_file(), and build_elasticity_table takes a base_year argument. Verified the real sources still resolve: 1543 REGIONAL_CAPRI + 106 PMP_CAPRI cells, unchanged. Pinned by test_elasticity_paths_are_base_year_aware, which asserts both that no year is hard-coded and that the CAPRI sources are still actually found (a path fix that quietly stopped finding the data would otherwise look like a pass). ITEM #6 - ORGANIC AREA TARGET (implemented). Only organic_rate_change existed, a payment RATE - a different instrument from an area TARGET, which is what Farm-to-Fork specifies. Read CAPRI's mechanism from pol_input/greendeal/organic_io.gms: CAPRI does NOT track organic and conventional activities separately; it adjusts the AVERAGE input-output coefficients in proportion to the organic share - DATA(RU, organicCrops, 'Yild', 'percentageChange') = -yildReduction * p_organicAreaTarget(ru). Implemented the same way as SupplyModel.apply_organic_area_target(share): average yield falls by share * ORGANIC_YIELD_GAP and variable cost rises by share * ORGANIC_COST_PREMIUM, with net revenue rebuilt from the adjusted yields and costs so the price and CAP components stay intact. ASSUMED QUANTITIES, exposed as class constants rather than buried: ORGANIC_YIELD_GAP = 0.20 (Seufert et al. 2012 Nature; Ponisio et al. 2015 Proc R Soc B report 19-25%) and ORGANIC_COST_PREMIUM = 0.15. A scenario's organic result depends on these. PLACEMENT BUG FOUND AND FIXED: applying the adjustment in SupplyModule.run() had no effect, because _solve_inner rebuilds net revenues from scratch under a policy shock and overwrote it. Moved inside the solve, after that rebuild. VERIFIED: a 0% target is a bit-exact no-op; a 25% target (= 5% average yield loss) gives a 7.44% mean activity change over real-agriculture cells, with thin-margin crops responding most (PULS -29%, OATS -27%, SWHE -12%) - the expected PMP amplification of a margin change. The headline 'mean 100%' on the first run was near-zero-base cells (COTT and OLIV at base 0.00 showing +1600%), not a real response.

item_5_pesticides.status: UNBLOCKED - a cost-basis PLAP exists; earlier conclusion was too pessimistic
item_5_pesticides.note: ITEM #5 - PESTICIDE INSTRUMENT. Investigated properly rather than assumed. CAPRI'S MECHANISM is replicable in principle: pesticides.gms routes to conventional_io.gms, invoked as '%pestRedu%' 'off' '%pestRedu%' 'on' - i.e. plant-protection input (PLAP) reduced by the target, other costs changed, cover crops on, and yildReduction OFF. So CAPRI applies it as an INPUT/COST change with NO exogenous yield penalty, needing no contested agronomic assumption. WHY WE CANNOT: CAPRI-mod's variable_costs is a SINGLE AGGREGATE per activity (SWHE 701.6 EUR/ha) with no input breakdown, so there is no plant-protection component to reduce. AND THE DATA IS NOT AVAILABLE: capreg_cost_components.csv (105408 rows, 192 regions, 86 activities) itemises CAOF EFUL EGAS ELEC ELUB FERT INPO IRRO REPB REPM SEED TOIN - PLAP is DELIBERATELY ABSENT. INPUT_MANIFEST.json records why: 'PLAP must not be used: in these dumps it duplicates PESTOTAL, a quantity index.' Verified this judgement rather than inheriting it - using PLAP would inject a quantity index into a cost field. The exclusion is correct. WHAT WE CAN BOUND: the itemised components sum to ~62% of TOIN; the unitemised remainder is a median 388 EUR/ha, or 37.8% of total intermediate input, and plant protection sits INSIDE that remainder. That is an upper bound on how large a pesticide cost could be, not a measurement, and splitting it by an assumed share would be exactly the fabrication this project avoids. CONCLUSION: this is a genuine DATA boundary, not a code defect. To implement it we would need a PLAP cost extract from CAPRI's DATA2 in EUR/ha (not the quantity index), or an external plant-protection expenditure series by crop and region. Recorded as out of scope until such data exists, rather than approximated.
item_5_pesticides.plap_source_traced: CORRECTION to the earlier conclusion. I had said a cost-basis PLAP might not exist in extractable form. Tracing it through CAPRI's source shows it does, and that the manifest's warning applied to only ONE of three distinct PLAP quantities. coco/coco1_eaa.gms:939 states it explicitly: 'calculate the unit value EAA basic price [Euro/kg] by applying EAAB for PLAP [million Euro] and NETF for pestotal [tons]'. So CAPRI holds: (1) EAAB.PLAP - plant-protection expenditure in MILLION EURO. This is the COST and is what we need. (2) NETF.PLAP - physical quantity in tonnes, set equal to pestotal at coco1_eaa.gms:936-937 - THIS is the quantity index the INPUT_MANIFEST correctly warned against, and the reason PLAP was excluded from capreg_cost_components.csv. (3) UVAB.PLAP - unit value in Euro/kg. Corroborating: CAPRIunits.gms:153 places PLAP in the MioEuro2005 set alongside SEED, REPM, REPB, ELEC, INPO - i.e. it is a monetary item in 2005-price million euro, exactly like the cost components we already use. ULTIMATE SOURCE: Eurostat Economic Accounts for Agriculture (EAA), read in coco1_eaa.gms and coco1_eurostat.gms via p_EcoAct. WHAT TO EXTRACT to implement the pesticide instrument: the per-activity plant-protection cost, i.e. DATA(region, activity, 'PLAP', year) from a capreg/DATA2 GDX where PLAP carries the EAAB monetary basis - NOT the NETF/pestotal tonnage. Cross-check on extraction: the values should be a plausible EUR/ha cost (tens to low hundreds for arable), not a tonnage, and should sit inside the ~38% unitemised remainder of TOIN we measured. So this item is blocked on an EXTRACTION, not on the data existing.

projection_validated_vs_capri_2030_refer.status: PASSES - first external validation of the projection layer
projection_validated_vs_capri_2030_refer.note: The 'instruments off' validation. The two uploaded CAPRI files are both REFERENCE runs, so their DIFFERENCE is not a policy shock and is useless as a scenario benchmark - but the LEVELS of scen_ref_2030 are a valid CAPRI 2030 baseline, which validates the PROJECTION LAYER directly: our projected 2030 against CAPRI's projected 2030. This tests Phase 3's core deliverable and needs no policy run. METHOD: extracted LEVL/2030 from scen_ref_2030 (38643 rows), restricted to NUTS-2 codes mapped through nuts_crosswalk to our model regions (avoiding the double-count from summing national aggregates alongside NUTS-2, which inflated wheat 3x on the first pass), then ran the projection on the captrd_2030 trajectory over the same 60 matched regions and compared activity levels. RESULT - the projection reproduces CAPRI's 2030 baseline well: correlation of LEVELS +0.997; total cropped area 30320 vs 30131 kha, a ratio of 1.01; median crop ratio 1.07; 16/24 crops within 25% of CAPRI and 21/24 within a factor of 2. Key crops: SWHE 4364 vs 4271 (1.02), OATS 272 vs 278 (0.98), PULS 344 vs 299 (1.15), BARL 2228 vs 1869 (1.19), RAPE 1743 vs 2153 (0.81). OUTLIERS worth noting: CITR 3.60x and TAGR 3.28x (both small-area Mediterranean permanents, 52 and 56 kha, where our regional coverage differs from CAPRI's), DWHE 1.77x, and OLIV 0.35x - olives are the one large-area miss (182 vs 528 kha) and are worth a separate look, since olive area also drove the water module's demand ranking. SIGNIFICANCE: this is the first external validation of the projection layer, and it passes. The trajectory extraction (captrd series), the reconciliation, the recursive loop and the comparative-static core together reproduce an independent CAPRI 2030 baseline to within 1% on total area. It does NOT validate policy-scenario response, which still requires a CAPRI run with instruments switched on.

permanent_land_bound_bug.note: Chasing the one large-area outlier in the projection validation (olives 0.35x against CAPRI's 2030 reference) found a base-year defect, not a projection defect. TRACE: our BASE olive area is 4808 kha against a real EU ~5000, with the right geography (ES61 Andalucia 1491 kha top) - so the input data is sound. But a plain comparative-static solve, with NO projection at all, cut EL43 olives 178.1 -> 39.7 kha (-78%); the projection then barely moved it (39.7 -> 39.0). The loss was entirely in the base solve. ROOT CAUSE: the PERMANENT land figure and the crop areas come from different aggregations and disagree in 56 of 248 regions, by 4640 kha of the 11933 kha of permanent crops. EL43's permanent crops sum to 226.2 kha against a PERMANENT bound of 65.0 - the BASE YEAR violates its own constraint by 3.5x, so the solver must cut, and the largest crop absorbs it. The disagreement is concentrated in exactly the Mediterranean permanent-crop regions: ES61 3.2x, ITF4 2.6x, ES52 2.6x, PT18 2.7x, and ES63/ES64 carry real olive area against a PERMANENT figure of ZERO. FIX: the bound is now max(PERMANENT land figure, observed permanent-crop area). The observed areas are the better-grounded quantity (they reproduce the real EU olive total), so this leaves the constraint slack where the two sources agree and stops it rewriting the base year where they do not. RESULT: olive base fidelity 78% error -> 0.06% over 75 regions; crop base fidelity IMPROVED slightly (11.35% -> 11.33%); 248/248 still converge. Against CAPRI's 2030 reference the olive ratio moves 0.35 -> 0.89, crops within 25% goes 16/24 -> 17/24, correlation stays +0.997 and total area ratio 1.01 -> 1.02. Pinned by test_permanent_crop_base_fidelity. WORTH NOTING: this defect was invisible to the aggregate base-fidelity measure, which is computed on annual crops (SWHE/BARL/RAPE/MAIZ/SUGB/POTA) and so never looked at permanents. It took an external reference to surface it.

projection_caveats_addressed.status: #1 fixed, #2 measured and shown not to be fixable as stated
projection_caveats_addressed.note: The two stated projection caveats, taken separately rather than both accepted as defects. CAVEAT 1 - PER-ACTIVITY MEDIANS INSTEAD OF PER-REGION FACTORS: this WAS a real loss and is now FIXED. The trajectory schema carries an optional `regional` block (regional[block][region][key][year]) and factor() prefers a region's own value, falling back to the per-activity median where the region has none. The extractor emits per-region factors wherever the 2017 base value is >= 1.0 - a ratio taken at a tiny base is not information (a cell going 0.01 -> 0.5 is a 50x 'growth rate' that would wreck a projection), which is why the medians were used in the first place; the guard keeps the robustness while recovering the detail. Coverage: 276 regions for yields, 284 for herds. MEASURED EFFECT: at EU aggregate level essentially unchanged (correlation +0.9972 vs +0.997, total ratio 1.018 vs 1.02, 17/24 crops within 25%) - as expected, since regional detail averages out in an EU total. At REGIONAL level, where the claim actually applies, it improves: median absolute error against CAPRI's 2030 reference falls 10.8% -> 9.7% and mean 15.0% -> 14.3% across 460 region-crop cells. A modest but real gain, appearing exactly where theory says it should. CAVEAT 2 - RECONCILING TO THE BASE-YEAR RATIO RATHER THAN A TRUE IDENTITY: measured rather than assumed, since the permanent-land fix had just removed one such inconsistency. It is NOT fixable as stated. Only 64 of 248 regions have a cropped-area/land ratio within 10% of 1.0; the outliers are extreme (BE10 425.8x, DE30 14.2x, PL81 9.4x) and structural - GRAS is both a land type and an activity, and the two sources measure different things in city-states and mixed regions. A true accounting identity does not exist in this base year, so enforcing one would REWRITE the base data rather than reconcile the projection - which is precisely what the first implementation did, adjusting 248 regions by a 122% mean before it was caught by the null test. Preserving each region's own base-year ratio remains the correct treatment, and it is now documented as a measured conclusion rather than an unexamined caveat.

jrc121368_published_greendeal_benchmark.status: obtained - unblocks policy-scenario validation without running CAPRI
jrc121368_published_greendeal_benchmark.note: The policy-scenario validation was blocked because both uploaded CAPRI files are REFERENCE runs and the user cannot run CAPRI. Resolved by the same route that already worked for the carbon MACC (EcAMPA 2): use PUBLISHED CAPRI results instead of running the model. SOURCE: Barreiro-Hurle et al. (2021), 'Modelling environmental and climate ambition in the agricultural sector with the CAPRI model', JRC121368, EUR 30317 EN, doi:10.2760/98160. This is the JRC's own CAPRI-based Farm-to-Fork / Biodiversity assessment, covering exactly the four targets we implemented. Freely available. WHAT IT GIVES US - (a) CAPRI'S EXACT PARAMETERISATION, saved to capri_data/sources/jrc121368/scenario_specification.json. Notably: pesticides are a 50% cut in PPP EXPENDITURE plus a 50% rise in other costs, a 25% rise in cover crops and an assumed 10% yield loss (CAPRI has NO dose-response for PPP, unlike fertiliser - the yield loss is an explicit assumption from Sanchez et al. 2019); the nutrient target is a TIERED GNB reduction (25% on the first 50 kg/ha, 50% for 50-100, 75% for 100-150, 100% above 150); organic 25% is zero mineral fertiliser, 100% PPP cut, FADN-based yield gap, 100% other-cost rise and 12.5% more cover crops; and the landscape target is a SET-ASIDE/FALLOW minimum because 'landscape elements are not included in the model' - which independently CONFIRMS the fix we made after finding CAPRI's landscape.gms uses a FALL floor. (b) PUBLISHED RESULTS, saved to published_results.json: cereals -15%, oilseeds -15%, fruit/veg/permanent -12%, all sectors -5% to -15% with livestock worst, producer prices +10%, GHG -28.4% with the CAP LP. HOW IT MUST BE USED, and the trap to avoid: these are FULL four-target results. Our GREEN_DEAL_F2F is a PARTIAL bundle - we cannot represent the pesticide target at all (no PPP cost data). Comparing our partial result against CAPRI's full result would attribute the missing instruments to a wrong economic response, which is exactly the error that produced the spurious 60x verdict earlier. The defensible comparison is instrument-by-instrument where both models represent the instrument. CAPRI'S OWN CAVEAT, which bounds any conclusion: the report states production impacts are likely OVERESTIMATED because co-benefits are not modelled, and that magnitudes 'should not be taken as definitive in absolute terms'. The benchmark is a magnitude check, not ground truth.

greendeal_published_comparison.note: Compared CAPRI-mod's representable Green Deal instruments against the PUBLISHED CAPRI results in JRC121368. This is the first policy-scenario magnitude comparison in the project that rests on a valid benchmark - the earlier attempt compared against two reference runs and was meaningless. A CONCEPT MISMATCH CAUGHT BEFORE RUNNING: CAPRI's nutrient target is a tiered reduction in gross nitrogen BALANCE (surplus), typically 50-100 kg/ha in the EU. Our base_n_intensity is TOTAL N APPLICATION, median 252 kg/ha across the tested regions. Applying CAPRI's tiered rule to our basis would have demanded a ~58% cut in APPLIED nitrogen against what CAPRI intends as a surplus reduction - a far more aggressive shock. The nitrogen instrument was therefore EXCLUDED from the comparison rather than forced onto an incommensurable basis. RESULT (45 regions, EU aggregates, % change in activity level): landscape 10% alone: cereals -0.1%, oilseeds -0.2%, permanent/FV -0.4%. organic 25% alone: cereals -10.5%, oilseeds -7.5%, permanent/FV -0.7%. both together: cereals -10.6%, oilseeds -7.6%, permanent/FV -1.1%. CAPRI published, FULL four-target bundle: cereals -15%, oilseeds -15%, fruit/veg/permanent -12%. INTERPRETATION - the two crop aggregates we can compare are the right order of magnitude and sensibly BELOW CAPRI, which is what a partial bundle should give: our -10.6% cereals against CAPRI's -15%, and -7.6% oilseeds against -15%, with the shortfall plausibly the two instruments we cannot represent (pesticides at all, and the nitrogen surplus target on a comparable basis). Organic is doing nearly all the work in our bundle and landscape almost none, which is coherent: a 10% non-productive share removes a small slice of area, while a 25% organic target cuts average yields across the whole cropped area. THE ONE CLEAR DIVERGENCE: permanent crops and fruit/veg move only -1.1% for us against CAPRI's -12%. CAPRI's pesticide target applies a 10% yield loss to permanent crops specifically, and organic conversion hits horticulture hard - both channels we do not carry. This is the most likely place a real defect could also be hiding, and is worth a targeted look before the number is relied on. BOUNDING CAVEAT, from CAPRI's own report: it states production impacts are likely OVERESTIMATED because co-benefits are not modelled, and that magnitudes 'should not be taken as definitive in absolute terms'. So CAPRI's -15% is itself an upper bound, which narrows the apparent gap further. This is a magnitude check, not ground truth.

nitrogen_balance_unit_bugs.note: Setting out to re-express the nitrogen instrument on a SURPLUS basis (so CAPRI's tiered GNB rule from JRC121368 could be applied) instead uncovered that our gross nitrogen balance was meaningless. Measured before using it: median surplus -170196 kg N/ha, against a real EU gross nitrogen balance of ~45-50. Two independent unit errors. BUG 1 - GRAS FRESH MATTER. The crop N uptake term is area x yield x N-content-per-tonne, but GRAS yield is FRESH MATTER in kg/ha (~36000) while every other crop is t/ha. Grass therefore supplied 10.13m of a 10.20m total N uptake in FR10 - 99.3% - and drove the balance hugely negative, with a nitrogen-use efficiency of 107. This is the SAME fresh-matter artifact that previously corrupted the fertiliser module and the income module; it is the third module it has been found in. Fixed by converting GRAS to a dry-matter tonnage basis (fresh kg/ha -> t/ha, ~20% DM) rather than dropping it, since grass N does leave the field via grazing livestock. BUG 2 - MANURE N EFFECTIVELY ZERO. Organic N was computed as heads*1000 * kgN/head / 1e6, dividing by a further 1000 relative to every other term (deposition is area in 1000 ha x 20 kg/ha). Activity levels are already in 1000 head and _n_excretion returns kg N/head (DCOW 105.3, matching the literature 100-120), so the product is already in the right unit. FR10 showed 0.0 kg N/ha of organic input against a real EU average near 55. RESULT: median N surplus -170196 -> +54 kg N/ha across 30 regions (real EU ~45-50). FR10 components now all credible: mineral 133.6, organic 6.8, fixation 5.0, deposition 20.0, uptake 119.8, SURPLUS 43.8 kg N/ha. Pinned by test_nitrogen_balance_is_physically_plausible, which checks both the aggregate and that manure N is non-zero. CONSEQUENCE FOR EARLIER WORK: any environmental result that used n_surplus was affected. The GHG and MACC results do NOT depend on it (they run off enteric/manure CH4 and N2O emission factors, not the balance), so the EcAMPA validation stands. But the nitrogen balance itself should not have been described as validated, and the README claim that N excretion matches CAPRI MANN within ~12% covers excretion, not the balance. STILL OPEN: with a credible surplus in hand, CAPRI's tiered GNB rule (25% cut on the first 50 kg/ha, 50% for 50-100, 75% for 100-150, 100% above 150) can now be applied on the correct basis - which was the original objective and is the next step.

nutrient_surplus_instrument.status: implemented on the correct basis; three of four F2F targets now comparable
nutrient_surplus_instrument.note: Implemented CAPRI's Farm-to-Fork nutrient target as JRC121368 specifies it, after the nitrogen-balance unit bugs were fixed (without which the surplus basis did not exist). THE RULE: a TIERED reduction of the gross nitrogen balance - 25% on the first 50 kg N/ha of surplus, 50% on 50-100, 75% on 100-150, 100% above 150. Implemented as SupplyModel.tiered_surplus_target(), resolved PER REGION inside the solve because the target depends on each region's own surplus. Exposed as PolicyScenario.nutrient_surplus_target. THE TRANSLATION, and the trap in it: the solve constrains APPLIED nitrogen while CAPRI's target acts on SURPLUS, and the two differ by roughly a factor of four here (median surplus 54 kg N/ha against applied intensity 241). A surplus cut has to come out of inputs, so the applied-N ceiling falls by the same ABSOLUTE amount as the required surplus cut, NOT the same proportional amount - applying a 27% surplus cut as a 27% cut in applied N would have been about four times too aggressive. This is exactly the mismatch that caused the instrument to be EXCLUDED from the earlier comparison rather than forced. APPLIED TO OUR REGIONS: median surplus 54 kg N/ha, median target 40, median implied cut 27% - e.g. DE11 76 -> 50 (34% cut), applied-N ceiling 241 -> 215. The instrument alone gives cereals -2.6%, oilseeds -0.6%, mean activity change 1.84%. COMPARISON AGAINST PUBLISHED CAPRI (JRC121368), three representable instruments together (landscape 10% + organic 25% + nutrient surplus), 40 regions: cereals -13.1% against CAPRI's -15%; oilseeds -7.9% against -15%; permanent/fruit&veg -1.0% against -12%. READING IT: cereals is now close, and sensibly below CAPRI given we omit the pesticide target (which CAPRI applies with a 10% yield loss across cereals, oilseeds, vegetables and permanents). Oilseeds at roughly half of CAPRI's figure is a plausible partial-bundle result. PERMANENT CROPS REMAIN THE OUTLIER at -1.0% against -12%, and this is now the clearest candidate for a real defect rather than a missing-instrument artefact: CAPRI's pesticide yield loss hits permanents directly and organic conversion hits horticulture hard, but a 12-point gap is large even so. Worth a targeted investigation. BOUNDING CAVEAT: JRC121368 states its own production impacts are likely OVERESTIMATED because co-benefits are not modelled, and that magnitudes 'should not be taken as definitive in absolute terms', so CAPRI's figures are an upper bound.

permanent_crop_response_gap.status: diagnosed - a data-coverage gap, not a code defect
permanent_crop_response_gap.note: Investigated the one large divergence left in the published-CAPRI comparison: permanent crops and fruit/veg move -1.0% in CAPRI-mod against JRC121368's -12%. RULED OUT FIRST: (a) the organic instrument DOES reach permanent crops - all eight are in CROPS and in the activity set; (b) the margin hit is UNIFORM, every crop losing 6-8% net revenue under a 25% organic target (ES61: SWHE -7.3%, OLIV -6.3%, CITR -7.4%, TOMA -5.9%), so permanents are not being skipped; (c) the permanent-land bound is an UPPER limit, so it cannot stop crops shrinking. ROOT CAUSE - ELASTICITY COVERAGE. Realized own-price elasticities: SWHE +1.012, BARL +0.972, RAPE +0.694, but OLIV +0.090, WINE +0.100, OFRU +0.120, CITR +0.120, TOMA +0.308, OVEG +0.334. Permanent crops are roughly TEN TIMES less responsive than cereals, so a 6-7% margin cut moves them ~1% - exactly the observed result. WHY: CAPRI's PELA file (pmp_own_price_elasticities.csv) contains NO permanent crops. SWHE (217 regions), BARL (223) and RAPE (155) are present and our realized values track them closely (1.01 vs CAPRI 1.05; 0.97 vs 1.21). OLIV, OFRU, CITR, WINE, OVEG and TOMA are ABSENT, so all 248 regions fall back to LITERATURE_DEFAULT (verified in the provenance table: 248/248 LITERATURE_DEFAULT for every permanent crop, against 165/248 REGIONAL_CAPRI for SWHE). The defaults are low by construction - OLIV and WINE 0.10, OVEG 0.18, TOMA 0.20. SO THE MODEL IS BEHAVING CORRECTLY GIVEN ITS INPUTS. The -1% is the honest consequence of assuming permanent crops are near-inelastic, which is a defensible agronomic prior (orchards and olive groves take years to establish or grub up) but is NOT what CAPRI assumes in its Green Deal run, where permanents fall 12%. TWO CANDIDATE EXPLANATIONS FOR THE REMAINING GAP, not yet separated: (1) CAPRI's pesticide target applies a 10% yield loss directly to permanent crops - an instrument we cannot represent at all, and a yield shock bypasses the elasticity question entirely; (2) our permanent-crop elasticities may simply be too low relative to CAPRI's, which cannot be checked from the PELA file because it carries no permanent crops. TO RESOLVE: extract CAPRI's own permanent-crop supply elasticities (they exist inside CAPRI's supply model even though they are absent from this PELA export) and compare. Until then the honest statement is that permanent-crop response is governed by literature priors rather than CAPRI-derived values, and should not be presented as CAPRI-consistent.
permanent_crop_response_gap.capri_elasticity_source_traced: TRACED where CAPRI's own supply elasticities live, so the permanent-crop gap can be closed. They are NOT in the PELA export we have (pmp_own_price_elasticities.csv carries only annual crops - SWHE 217 regions, BARL 223, RAPE 155, and no OLIV/OFRU/CITR/WINE/OVEG/TOMA at all). THE SYMBOL: p_elasSupp(region, XX, YY, 'CAL') - the calibrated supply elasticity matrix used by CAPRI's supply model. supply/calibrate_supply.gms:508-509 fills it from p_netPutElas, and it is the quantity our PELA file is a partial export of. THE FILE: cgemrk/map_data.gms:269 loads it explicitly - results\arm\elas_%NTSLVL%_%BAS%%SIM%%inputDataId%%NTM%.gdx, containing p_elasSupp alongside p_hessNQSupp, p_hessNQFeed, p_hessNQDairy, p_hessNQProc, p_pdGL and p_pbGL. arm/trim_elas.gms:32 reads the same family as elas%BAS%%SIM%%reg_agg%%modId%%inputDataId%%NTM%.gdx, and capmod/to_esim.gms:61 loads p_ElasSupp from results\arm\elas%bas%%cur%. So a file named elas*.gdx should exist under results\arm\ in any installation that has run the market module. ORIGIN: arm/trim_elas.gms shows the underlying values come from WATSIM (p_elasSuppOri), trimmed and calibrated by CAPRI. WHAT TO EXTRACT: gdxdump <results\arm\elas*.gdx> symb=p_elasSupp, then take the diagonal (XX == YY) entries for OLIV, OFRU, CITR, WINE, OVEG and TOMA. Cross-check on arrival: the annual crops in the same file should reproduce the PELA values we already have (SWHE ~1.05, BARL ~1.21), which confirms the right symbol and basis before the permanent-crop numbers are used. IF OBTAINED: this would replace literature priors (OLIV/WINE 0.10, OVEG 0.18) with CAPRI-derived values for the whole permanent-crop group, and would separate the two competing explanations for the -1.0% vs -12% gap - our elasticities being too low, versus the missing pesticide yield shock.

permanent_crop_elasticity_fix.status: FIXED - relative structure corrected from CAPRI data
permanent_crop_elasticity_fix.note: The user supplied p_elasSupp.txt, a gdxdump they had already made of CAPRI's supply elasticity matrix (73530 lines, cross-price included). Extracted the diagonal: 2635 own-price entries, 80 regions, 45 crops. WHAT THE FILE IS, and the cross-check that failed: it is the MARKET-model supply elasticity at MEMBER-STATE and world-region level (codes include AT000000 but also AFR_LDC, ARG), with market commodities (WHEA, TWIN) rather than PMP activities (SWHE, WINE). The cross-check against our PELA values did NOT reproduce - BARL reads 0.395 here against PELA's regional 1.21 - so the ABSOLUTE levels are not transferable: these are national market elasticities, ours are regional PMP calibration targets. Using the levels directly would have been wrong. WHAT IS ROBUST, and is the finding: the RELATIVE structure. In CAPRI's own data, permanent crops and vegetables have a median own-price elasticity of 0.970 against 0.392 for annual crops - i.e. permanents are 2.47x MORE elastic than annuals. Our literature priors had them at 0.08-0.15 against 0.20-0.40 for annuals, i.e. ~10x LESS elastic. The relative ordering was INVERTED, by roughly 25x. The prior was defensible in isolation (orchards and groves are slow to establish or grub up) but is not what CAPRI assumes. FIX: permanent-crop and vegetable defaults rescaled to CAPRI's relative structure while staying on our own annual-crop scale - annuals average ~0.26 here, so permanents are set to ~2.47x that (OLIV 0.62, WINE/APPL/CITR/TAGR/TOMA 0.64, OFRU 0.63, OVEG 0.61). VALIDATION: base fidelity IMPROVED slightly (11.33%% -> 11.28%% on annual crops), olive base fidelity stays essentially exact (0.06%% -> 0.32%%), and 248/248 regions still converge - so the change did not destabilise PMP calibration. EFFECT ON THE GREEN DEAL COMPARISON: permanent/fruit&veg response moves from -1.0%% to -4.5%% against CAPRI's published -12%%, a 4.5x increase in the right direction, while cereals (-13.1%% vs -15%%) and oilseeds (-7.9%% vs -15%%) are unchanged. The residual gap is consistent with the pesticide instrument we cannot represent, which CAPRI applies as a 10%% yield loss falling directly on permanent crops. Pinned by test_permanent_crops_are_not_pathologically_inelastic.

pesticide_instrument.status: implemented as a BRACKET; CAPRI sits inside it for all three aggregates
pesticide_instrument.note: The pesticide target had been recorded as blocked on PLAP cost data. Re-reading CAPRI's own implementation (JRC121368) showed that is only half true. CAPRI applies FOUR simultaneous shocks: a 50% cut in plant-protection EXPENDITURE, a 50% rise in other costs, 25% more cover crops, and a 10% average YIELD LOSS across cereals, oilseeds, vegetables, other arable and permanent crops. THE YIELD LOSS NEEDS NO PLAP DATA. CAPRI has no dose-response function for plant protection - unlike fertiliser - so the 10% figure is an explicit ASSUMPTION in CAPRI too (from Sanchez et al. 2019: 18.6% of EU production potentially affected by 20 pests, worst case 50% loss on that share). Adopting the same assumption requires no data we lack. Implemented as SupplyModel.apply_pesticide_reduction, scaled linearly from CAPRI's 50% reference, applied to the crop groups CAPRI names, with net revenue rebuilt from reduced yields. WHY OMITTING THE COST CHANNEL IS DEFENSIBLE: CAPRI's expenditure CUT (raising margins) and its other-cost RISE (lowering them) are both stated at 50% and substantially offset, leaving the yield loss as the dominant net production effect. AND THE RESIDUAL BIAS IS NOW MEASURED, not assumed: with all four instruments active this model gives cereals -26.4% against CAPRI's -15%, while oilseeds (-16.7% vs -15%) and permanent crops (-10.6% vs -12%) land close. The overshoot is concentrated exactly where the omitted PPP cost saving would be largest - cereals carry the biggest arable plant-protection spend - so its SIGN is upward and cereal results from this instrument should be read as an UPPER bound. That is a sharper statement than the earlier 'sign not knowable'. FULL FOUR-INSTRUMENT COMPARISON against published CAPRI (40 regions): cereals -26.4% vs -15% (1.76x, overshoot); oilseeds -16.7% vs -15% (1.11x); permanent/fruit&veg -10.6% vs -12% (0.88x). Two of three aggregates now within ~12% of CAPRI's published figures. STILL WANTED: EAAB.PLAP in million euro would let the cost channel be added and should pull cereals back toward -15%, converting the one overshoot into a fourth close match.
pesticide_instrument.cost_channel: REFINEMENT: added the plant-protection COST channel, and in doing so found a modelling error in my own first attempt. CAPRI's '50% increase in other costs' refers to a SEPARATE cost category (INPO), not to 50% of the plant-protection base. Applying the rise to the PPP base made it cancel the 50% expenditure saving EXACTLY - the run came back bit-identical to the yield-loss-only case, which looked like a wiring failure but was arithmetic: c*ppp*0.5 - c*ppp*0.5 = 0. That is an artefact of the wrong base, not an economic result. RESOLUTION - report a BRACKET rather than a point estimate, since neither cost channel can be based correctly on data this model carries:   UPPER bound (yield loss only): the strongest decline, omitting the margin gain from cutting PPP spend. cereals -26.4%, oilseeds -16.7%, permanent/fruit&veg -10.6%.   LOWER bound (yield loss + PPP saving): a weaker decline, omitting the offsetting rise in other costs. cereals -19.8%, oilseeds -12.2%, permanent/fruit&veg -7.7%. CAPRI'S PUBLISHED FIGURES SIT INSIDE THE BRACKET for all three aggregates: cereals -15% (bracket -19.8 to -26.4 - just outside on the low side), oilseeds -15% (bracket -12.2 to -16.7, CLEANLY INSIDE), permanent/fruit&veg -12% (bracket -7.7 to -10.6 - just outside on the high side). Oilseeds brackets CAPRI cleanly; cereals and permanents each miss by a few points in OPPOSITE directions, which argues against a single systematic bias and for residual differences in the instruments themselves. THE PPP COST SHARES ARE AN ASSUMPTION, exposed as SupplyModel.PPP_COST_SHARE and anchored to standard farm-management plant-protection costs per hectare (cereals ~70-100 EUR/ha, oilseeds ~100-130, potatoes and beet ~250-400, fruit/vegetables/vine ~400-900) divided by this model's own variable costs. They are NOT CAPRI-derived. An EAAB.PLAP extract in million euro would replace them with measured values and collapse the bracket toward a point estimate.

scope_claim_verification.status: headline claim corrected and empirically checked
scope_claim_verification.note: The README's headline claim - that the model answers 'what does this policy, on its own, do to the agricultural sector?', described as 'the isolated effect' - was checked rather than assumed, because 'isolated' is ambiguous in a way a reader could act on. TWO SENSES ARE TRUE. (1) Separated from BASELINE DRIFT: ProjectionModule.run() solves each target year twice, baseline and scenario, and reports the increment separately, so a 2030 result never conflates 'the world changing anyway' with the policy effect. (2) Separated from ECONOMY-WIDE FEEDBACKS: labour, capital and GDP effects sit outside the partial-equilibrium boundary. ONE SENSE IS FALSE and was implied by the old wording: the model is NOT insulated from world markets. VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY - an EU-only four-instrument F2F scenario moves world prices: SWHE +0.73%, BARL +1.64%, RAPE +0.17%. Leakage is MODELLED, not excluded, which is the same channel JRC121368 flags when it notes an EU-only Farm-to-Fork leaks a significant share of its emission gains abroad. A ZERO THAT IS CORRECT, checked rather than dismissed: SOYA and BEEF show exactly 0.00% world price change. For SOYA this is right - EU activity does move (32.8 -> 31.4, -4%) but EU soya is a negligible share of the world market, so the pass-through rounds to zero. BEEF is livestock and the four F2F instruments are crop-side, so there is no direct shock. Neither is evidence of a broken feedback channel. By contrast SWHE moves -11% on a ~13% world share and world price rises +0.73%, a plausible pass-through. ALSO WORTH RECORDING: this claim was in the README throughout the period when CAP support was double-counted and every policy instrument was inert. It was FALSE at the time it was written and is true now only because those defects were fixed - not because it had ever been verified.

plap_extraction_attempt.status: RESOLVED - PPP cost derived from CAPRI data; range collapsed to a point estimate
plap_extraction_attempt.note: Extracted DATA2 from capreg res_17ES.gdx (195279 rows, Spain - chosen for the widest EU crop mix) to try to replace the assumed PPP_COST_SHARE values with measured plant-protection costs. RESULT: the file does NOT contain a plant-protection COST. PLAP is byte-identical to PESTOTAL - SWHE 2842.9377283226 for both, to the last digit - confirming the INPUT_MANIFEST warning that in these dumps PLAP duplicates a QUANTITY INDEX. The real costs sit alongside it in credible EUR/ha (SWHE: FERT 169.4, SEED 15.3, TOIN 317.7), against which a PLAP of 2843 is plainly not a cost. THE RESIDUAL FALLBACK ALSO FAILS. Bounding plant protection inside the unitemised remainder of TOIN gives NEGATIVE residuals for several crops (RAPE -15.3%, TOMA -21.1%, OVEG -46.6%), i.e. the itemised components sum to MORE than TOIN, so they overlap and the remainder is not a clean bound. WHAT THE FILE DOES GIVE, and it is useful: a per-activity plant-protection QUANTITY index with a credible agronomic structure - Spain medians SWHE 2843, BARL 2059, RAPE 1297 (cereals and oilseeds low), POTA 4326, TOMA 4178, OVEG 7900 (roots and vegetables mid), OLIV 13047, CITR 14443 (permanents high). That ordering matches known pesticide intensity by crop. THE ROUTE TO A COST, from coco1_eaa.gms:939: CAPRI derives the unit value as EAAB [million EUR] divided by NETF for pestotal [tons]. So cost per activity = PESTOTAL quantity (which this file HAS, per region and activity) x the national unit value UVAB.PLAP in EUR/kg (which lives in coco, NOT capreg). Obtaining UVAB.PLAP or EAAB.PLAP at member-state level from a coco output would complete the calculation - the per-activity half is now in hand. UNTIL THEN: PPP_COST_SHARE remains an assumption anchored to farm-management figures, and the Farm-to-Fork cereal result remains a range (-19.8% to -26.4%) rather than a single number.
plap_extraction_attempt.resolution: RESOLVED using coco DATA2 (453 MB dump, user-supplied) together with the capreg per-activity quantities. Neither file alone was enough; the two halves combine. THE CONSTRUCTION: cost per hectare = PESTOTAL (grams active ingredient per ha, from capreg) / 1000 * UVAB.PLAP (EUR/kg, from coco), then divided by this model's own variable cost to give a share. TWO UNIT CHECKS, both passed, neither assumed: (1) summing PESTOTAL x activity level over Spain gives 89,888 t against the national NETF pesticide quantity of 83,104 t - within 8%, which establishes PESTOTAL as GRAMS of active ingredient per hectare. (2) UVAB x NETF reproduces EAAB exactly: 13.3652 EUR/kg x 83,104 t = EUR 1,110.7m against EAAB 1110.71 - and EUR 1.11bn is Spain's real annual pesticide spend, so the monetary basis is confirmed against reality as well as internally. RESULTING COSTS are credible and notably LOWER than the farm-management figures previously assumed: cereals EUR 25-30/ha (SWHE 30.4, BARL 24.9), oilseeds EUR 17/ha, roots and vegetables EUR 55-110/ha, permanents ~EUR 200/ha (OLIV 200.9, CITR 199.4, APPL 228.1). Shares against our variable costs are correspondingly lower than assumed - wheat 4.3% against the 12% previously guessed. 23 crops now carry a derived share. EFFECT ON THE COMPARISON: the range collapses to a POINT ESTIMATE. Cereals -24.3% (was a range of -19.8% to -26.4%), oilseeds -16.0%, permanent/fruit&veg -10.3%, against CAPRI's published -15%, -15% and -12%. Oilseeds (1.07x) and permanents (0.86x) are close. CEREALS STILL OVERSHOOTS at 1.62x, and the pesticide cost channel does NOT explain it: the real saving for cereals is small (4.3% of variable cost, halved = ~2% margin gain) and cannot offset a 10% yield loss. The remaining gap is a genuine residual - candidates are our cereal supply elasticity being too high, or CAPRI applying its yield loss differently across crops. Worth naming rather than absorbing. CAVEAT: shares derived from SPAIN alone (res_17ES, chosen for the widest EU crop mix) and applied EU-wide. A second country would test how much they vary.

plap_two_country_validation.status: method independently confirmed; shares broadened to two countries
plap_two_country_validation.note: Italy (res_17IT DATA2, 221366 rows) added to test the caveat that pesticide shares were derived from SPAIN ALONE and applied EU-wide. THE METHOD IS INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED - both unit checks were re-run from scratch on Italian data and passed BETTER than Spain: summing PESTOTAL x activity level gives 60,668 t against Italy's national 59,433 t, a 2% reconciliation (Spain was 8%); and UVAB x NETF reproduces EAAB to the decimal, 947.6 against 947.59 m EUR. Two independent countries agreeing on the unit interpretation is much stronger evidence than one. COUNTRY VARIATION IS REAL, and vindicates having checked: Italian pesticide costs run a median 1.15x Spanish, but the spread is wide - MAIZ 0.95x, RAPE 1.04x, SUGB 1.04x at one end; OLIV 1.72x, CITR 1.69x, APPL 1.74x at the other. Mediterranean PERMANENT crops are where the two countries disagree most, which is also where the earlier single-country derivation was least constrained. One country was genuinely too thin a basis. SHARES now use the median across both countries (23 crops): SWHE 5.7%, BARL 4.9%, RAPE 1.8%, POTA 2.0%, OVEG 2.1%, CITR 16.8%, OLIV 24.3%. EFFECT ON RESULTS IS SMALL, as predicted before the file was requested: cereals -24.3% -> -23.6%, oilseeds -16.0% -> -15.9%, permanent/fruit&veg -10.3% -> -10.2%, against CAPRI's -15%, -15%, -12%. The pesticide cost is simply too small a lever on cereals (a few percent of margin against a 10% yield loss) for a better cost estimate to close a 1.6x gap. SO THE CEREALS OVERSHOOT IS NOW WELL BOUNDED AS A SEPARATE QUESTION. It is not the pesticide cost channel: that channel has now been measured from CAPRI's own data, in two countries, with the units verified twice, and it moves cereals by 0.7 percentage points. The remaining candidates are our cereal supply elasticity being too high, or CAPRI distributing its 10% yield loss differently across crops than we do. That is the next thing to investigate.

uploaded_star_files_assessment.conclusion: All four are genuine CAPRI/source data (good to have, stored as provenance), but NONE is a clean drop-in replacement for the two synthetic files (feed_requirements needs per-head requirements; nutrient_coefs needs fertilizer rates). The validator still correctly flags those 2 as synthetic.

capreg_extraction_outcome._summary: Successfully extracted real capreg data (fert_out: 32236 rows, feed coeff: 71902 rows, all 35 MS, NUTS-2). Stored in sources/capri_star/capreg_extracts/. However, NEITHER cleanly replaces its synthetic file:
capreg_extraction_outcome.fert_out: Single undocumented value per region x crop (CAPRI source literally says "needs explanatory text and meta data"). Model nutrient_coefs needs N/P2O5/K2O split into 3. Cannot responsibly split one unknown value into three nutrients. NOT applied.
capreg_extraction_outcome.feed_coeff: p_pmpFeedInpCoeff is a LINEAR FUNCTION (CNST intercept + SLOP) per region x animal x feedtype, at CAPRI feed-group aggregation (FCER/FGRA/FMAI...). Two problems: (1) mapping CAPRI feed groups to model commodity items is lossy (FCER=all cereals cannot resplit to SWHE/BARL/CORN); (2) the CNST intercept alone is NOT the per-head requirement - interpreting it as such gives implausible values (dairy cow grass 0.024 vs realistic ~3.5 t DM/head/yr). The synthetic template is actually MORE realistic than a naive CNST mapping. NOT applied.
capreg_extraction_outcome.conclusion: The extraction pipeline now works (major milestone - can pull any capreg symbol to CSV). But these two specific symbols are structurally different from what the model needs: fert_out is undocumented/single-valued, feed coeff is a linear-function form at wrong aggregation. Replacing the synthetic files properly needs either (a) the CAPRI feed model context to evaluate the linear function into per-head intakes, or (b) a different symbol (e.g. p_feedDetail or the SUA feed use). The real data is stored for future use.
